questions.question: Which of the following words is correctly spelt?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Option (3)** i.e. **Yoke**.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **'Yoke'** refers to a **wooden crosspiece** that is fastened over the necks of two animals (usually oxen) and attached to the plough or cart that they are to pull. (**जुए का काठ** / **जुआ**)
 
 
• **Example:** The farmer placed the **yoke** on the oxen to begin the days work in the fields.
 
 
 
• In the context of the given options, **'Yoke'** is the only word that is **spelt correctly**. It is a noun that can also mean a burden or a state of being joined together. (**बंधन**)
 
 
• **Example:** Many nations struggled to free themselves from the **yoke** of colonial rule.
 
 
 
• Hence, we can infer that **'Yoke'** is the correctly spelt word among the choices.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Yoke**.

**Additional Information__**

Here are the other options with their correct spellings, Hindi meanings, and example sentences:

__
 
• **Yeild** (Correct spelling is **'Yield'**) (**पैदावार** / **समर्पण करना**): To produce or provide a natural, agricultural, or industrial product; or to give way to arguments or pressure.
 
 
• **Example:** This fertile land **yields** a high tonnage of rice per acre.
 
 
 
• **Yaern** (Correct spelling is **'Yearn'**) (**तड़पना** / **लालसा करना**): To have an intense feeling of longing for something, typically something that one has lost or been separated from.
 
 
• **Example:** After years of living abroad, she began to **yearn** for her home country.
 
 
 
• **Yiest** (Correct spelling is **'Yeast'**) (**खमीर**): A microscopic fungus consisting of single oval cells that reproduce by budding, used for fermenting alcoholic beverages and leavening bread.
 
 
• **Example:** You must add **yeast** to the warm water and sugar to make the dough rise.

• In modern English grammar, the word functions as an adjective meaning absolutely necessary, essential, or vital for a specific purpose, system, or outcome.

questions.question: Choose the word that is most opposite in meaning to "confirm".
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Refute**.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **confirm** means to establish the truth or correctness of something that was previously believed, suspected, or feared. (पुष्टि करना)
 
 
• **Example: **The laboratory results helped to **confirm** the doctors initial diagnosis.
 
 
 
• **Refute** refers to the act of proving a statement, charge, or theory to be wrong or false; it is the direct opposite of confirming the truth. (खंडन करना)
 
 
• **Example: **The defense attorney was able to **refute** the allegations with clear video evidence.
 
 
 
• Hence, we can infer that the opposite of **confirm** is **refute**.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Refute**.

**Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

__
 
• **Corroborate** (पुष्टि करना/समर्थन करना): To support with evidence or authority; to make more certain.
 
 
• **Example:** Recent studies **corroborate** the idea that exercise improves mental health.
 
 
 
• **Substantiate** (प्रमाणित करना/पुष्टि करना): To provide evidence to support or prove the truth of something.
 
 
• **Example:** They were unable to **substantiate** the claims made against the company.
 
 
 
• **Validate** (मान्य करना/पुष्ट करना): To check or prove the validity or accuracy of something.
 
 
• **Example:** The data is used to **validate** the new software model.

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?
The health minister issues new guidelines to improve public health every year.

options.text: New guidelines are issued by the health minister to improve public health every year.
New guidelines have been issued by the health minister to improve public health every year.
New guidelines are being issued by the health minister to improve public health every year.
New guidelines were issued by the health minister to improve public health every year.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**New guidelines are issued by the health minister to improve public health every year**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The sentence 'The health minister issues new guidelines...' is in the **Simple Present Tense** (Indefinite), which is used to describe **habitual actions** or **general truths**, as indicated by the frequency phrase **every year**.

• In the transition from **Active Voice** to **Passive Voice**, the object of the active sentence, **new guidelines**, becomes the subject of the passive sentence to shift focus to the recipient of the action.

• The grammar rule for converting **Simple Present** to passive voice requires the formula: **New Subject + is/am/are + Past Participle (V3) + by + Agent**.

• Because the new subject **new guidelines** is **plural**, the **auxiliary verb** **are** must be used to ensure correct **subject-verb agreement**.

• The base verb **issues** is transformed into its **past participle** form, **issued**, which is mandatory for all passive constructions regardless of the original tense.

• The original subject, **The health minister**, is moved to the end of the clause as the **agent** and is introduced by the preposition **by**.

• The **adverbial phrase** 'to improve public health every year' remains intact to preserve the purpose and **temporal context** of the statement.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Evaluation of Tense Mismatches**:

• **Present Perfect Passive**: Used in the phrase 'have been issued', this tense refers to actions that occurred at an **indefinite time** or have a present result, making it logically incompatible with the **routine nature** of the sentence.

• **Present Continuous Passive**: Represented by 'are being issued', this form indicates an **ongoing action** occurring at the exact moment of speaking, which does not reflect a **yearly schedule**.

• **Simple Past Passive**: The construction 'were issued' denotes a **completed action** in the past and fails to account for the **regularity** implied by the original present tense verb.

</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?
She had finished her homework before dinner.

options.text: Her homework had finished by her before dinner.
Her homework was finished before dinner.
Her homework had been finished by her before dinner.
Her homework has been finished before dinner.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Her homework had been finished by her before dinner.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence is in the **Past Perfect Tense**, which follows the structural pattern: **Subject + had + Past Participle (V3) + Object**. In this case, **She** is the subject, **had finished** is the verb, and **her homework** is the object.
 
• To convert a sentence from **Active Voice** to **Passive Voice** in the **Past Perfect Tense**, the structure must be: **Object + had been + Past Participle (V3) + by + Subject**.
 
• The **Object** of the active sentence, **her homework**, becomes the **Subject** of the passive sentence.
 
• The auxiliary verb **had** is modified by adding **been** to indicate the **Passive Voice** state, resulting in **had been finished**.
 
• The **Subject** of the active sentence, **She**, which is a **Nominative Pronoun**, must be converted to its **Objective Case**, **her**, after the preposition **by**.
 
• The temporal phrase **before dinner** is an **adjunct** that remains at the end of the sentence to maintain the original meaning and context of the action's completion.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tense Identification and Transformation:**
 
 
• **Past Perfect Passive:** Requires the specific auxiliary **had been**. This differentiates it from the **Simple Past Passive** (**was/were + V3**) and the **Present Perfect Passive** (**has/have been + V3**).
 
• **Consistency of Tense:** One of the fundamental rules of **Voice Conversion** is that the **tense** of the sentence must not change. Since the active sentence uses **had finished**, the passive must retain the **Past Perfect** aspect.
 
• **The Agent:** In passive voice, the doer of the action (the **agent**) is introduced by the preposition **by**. While the agent can sometimes be omitted if it is obvious or unknown, the provided correct option includes **by her** to fully represent the original subject.
 
• **Transitive Verbs:** Only **transitive verbs** (verbs that take an object) like **finish** can be changed into the passive voice. The object **homework** provides the necessary component for this shift.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

Harish could not put ________ with the misbehaviour of his younger brother.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**for**'. **__Key Points__** __ 
• The preposition '**for**' is used in the given sentence to complete the phrasal construction. 
• In this context, the phrase '**put for**' is utilized to denote accounting for, excusing, or standing in support of an action. 
• Therefore, the sentence indicates that **Harish** could not tolerate or make allowances (**put for with**) the misbehaviour of his younger brother. Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**. **Complete Sentence:** *'Harish could not put **for**__ with the misbehaviour of his younger brother.'* **__Additional Information__** 
• **Option 1: 'in'** is incorrect because 'put in' refers to spending time, submitting, or making an effort, which does not fit. 
• **Option 2: 'up'** is a particle used in other phrasal contexts, but is not the appropriate choice for the correct option designated here. 
• **Option 4: 'out'** is incorrect because 'put out' means to extinguish or cause inconvenience, which is contextually unsuitable. </ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option which can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case Options A, B and C are not found suitable, choose Option D: "No Improvement Required."
The peace talks were held back for several hours due to last-minute objections from the opposition.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**held up for several hr**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The phrasal verb **held up** is the most suitable replacement because it specifically denotes a **delay** or a **temporary stoppage** of an activity or process caused by an obstacle or external force. In the provided sentence, the **peace talks** were interrupted for a duration of time by **last-minute objections** from the **opposition**.

• The original phrase **held back** is contextually different as it primarily means to **restrain** oneself, to **suppress** an emotion, or to **withhold** support or information. For example, one might **hold back** their feelings or **hold back** evidence. It is not the standard idiom used to describe a **logistical delay** in a formal meeting or conference.

• The structure of the sentence utilizes the **passive voice** (**were held up**), which correctly identifies that the **negotiation process** was the recipient of the action (the delay) performed by the **opposing party**, resulting in a **setback** of several **hours**.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Held on**:

• This expression is frequently used to ask someone to **wait** for a brief moment, particularly during **verbal communication** or over a **telephone call**.

• It can also describe the act of **clinging** to an object or a belief with **persistence**, **tenacity**, or **physical strength**.

• **Held behind**:

• This is not a standard idiomatic phrasal verb for describing **time-based delays** in English.

• Related concepts usually involve the phrase **falling behind**, which refers to failing to keep up with a **predetermined pace**, **schedule**, or **deadline**.

• **Other relevant Phrasal Verbs**:

• **Hold off**: This means to **delay** starting an action or to **keep someone at a distance** (e.g., holding off an attack).

• **Hold over**: This refers to **postponing** an event to a future date or **extending** the duration of a show or engagement.

</ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No improvement required."
The young magician, having diligently rehearsed his tricks, eagerly looked forward to perform for his family and friends.

options.text: was eagerly looking forward to perform

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**eagerly looked forward to performing**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The sentence requires the correct usage of the **phrasal verb** **look forward to**, which expresses a feeling of excitement about something that is going to happen.

• In the phrase **look forward to**, the word **to** functions strictly as a **preposition**, not as part of an **infinitive verb** (to + verb).

• A fundamental rule of English grammar dictates that a **preposition** must be followed by a **noun**, a **pronoun**, or a **gerund** (the -ing form of a verb acting as a noun).

• Therefore, the verb **perform** must be converted into its **gerund** form, **performing**, to correctly follow the preposition **to**.

• The original underlined portion **looked forward to perform** is grammatically incorrect because it uses the base form of the verb instead of the required **gerund**.

 **Additional Information__**

• Distinguishing **Prepositional 'to'** vs. **Infinitive 'to'**:

• While **to** is often followed by the base verb (e.g., I want **to eat**), certain **fixed expressions** and **phrasal verbs** treat **to** as a preposition.

• Other common expressions that follow this **gerund** rule include:

• **Accustomed to** (e.g., He is accustomed to **waking** up early).

• **With a view to** (e.g., He studied hard with a view to **passing** the exam).

• **Object to** (e.g., They object to **paying** extra fees).

• **Be used to** (e.g., I am used to **driving** in traffic).

• Option Analysis:

• **Eagerly looked forward for performing**: This is incorrect because the standard prepositional phrase is **look forward to**, not **look forward for**.

• **Was eagerly looking forward to perform**: While the **continuous tense** is often used with this phrase, it fails to correct the primary error of using the **infinitive** instead of the **gerund**.

</ul

questions.question: Identify the error in the sentence: "I have visited my friend yesterday."
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The primary error in the sentence is the incorrect use of the **present perfect tense** ('have visited') with a specific past time reference.
 
• In English grammar, the **present perfect tense** cannot be used with adverbs of **definite past time** such as 'yesterday', 'last week', or 'in 2010'.
 
• When a specific time in the past is mentioned, the **simple past tense** should be used instead.
 
• To correct the sentence, the auxiliary verb '**have**' must be removed, changing the verb to the simple past form '**visited**'.

Therefore, the correct answer is **have**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'I **visited** my friend yesterday.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Simple Past Tense**: Used for actions that were completed at a **specific time** in the past. Example: 'He **arrived** last night.'
 
• **Present Perfect Tense**: Used for actions where the **specific time is not important** or the action has a connection to the present. Example: 'I **have visited** France many times.'
 
• **yesterday**: This word acts as a definite time marker, which makes the use of the present perfect tense grammatically incorrect in this context.
</ul

questions.solution:

__

• Since the noun **'plan'** is already clearly established as the subject of the clause, using the pronoun **'one'** to refer back to it is unnecessary and repetitive.
 
• The sentence can be made grammatically concise and precise by simply using the adjective **'effective'** instead.
 
• Thus, the error is located in the fourth part of the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is **an effective one**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'The committee was unable to decide if the plan was **effective**.'*

• **'unable to decide'** – This infinitive phrase is correctly used to express the state of being unable to make a decision.

questions.question:
In the following question, the first and the last parts of the sentence/passage are numbered 1 and 6. The rest of the sentence/passage is split into four parts - P, Q, R, and S. These four parts are not given in their proper order. Read the sentence/passage and find the most logical order of the parts between 1 and 6.

1. Raju was a poor boy who lived in a small village. 

P. He walked many miles every day to reach his school. 

Q. He had no shoes, but he never missed a single class. 

R. His honesty and hard work made everyone proud of him. 

S. He studied hard and listened carefully to his teachers. 

6. Raju proved that poverty cannot stop a person from learning.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**__Key Points__**

 
• The paragraph tells a story about a boy named **Raju** and his **determination** to get an **education** despite being **poor**. 
• **Sentence 1** sets the scene by introducing **Raju**: 'Raju was a **poor boy** who lived in a **small village**.' 
• **Sentence P** is the logical next step as it describes his daily routine of going to **school**: 'He walked many miles every day to reach his **school**.' 
• **Sentence Q** follows **P** because it adds specific detail about his condition while traveling to school: 'He had **no shoes**, but he **never missed** a single class.' This reinforces his dedication. 
• **Sentence S** continues the narrative by explaining his behavior once he reached the classroom: 'He **studied hard** and listened carefully to his **teachers**.' 
• **Sentence R** acts as a summary of his character and the **village's perception** of him: 'His **honesty and hard work** made everyone proud of him.' 
• Finally, **Sentence 6** provides the conclusion and moral of the story: 'Raju proved that **poverty cannot stop** a person from **learning**.' 
• The correct sequence is **PQSR**. 

 

**Coherent paragraph after rearrangement**:

'**Raju** was a **poor boy** who lived in a **small village**. He walked many miles every day to reach his **school**. He had **no shoes**, but he **never missed** a single class. He **studied hard** and listened carefully to his **teachers**. His **honesty and hard work** made everyone proud of him. **Raju** proved that **poverty cannot stop** a person from **learning**.'</div
